overview: Persia here means Iran during Qajar consolidation and rule. Its imported dates, 1783 to 1920, are map coverage limits: Qajar consolidation continued through 1794 and the founder’s coronation in 1796, while the dynasty ended in 1925. Some outlines extend too far into the Caucasus for their displayed dates. They should not be treated as precise borders after the nineteenth-century wars with Russia.

periods.title: Contested power and Qajar consolidation
periods.summary: The Qajars defeated the last Zand ruler in 1794; Agha Mohammad Khan was crowned in 1796.

periods.title: Kingship and foreign pressure
periods.summary: The new dynasty faced wars with Russia and major territorial losses in the Caucasus.

periods.title: New schools and technologies
periods.summary: Dar al-Fonun opened in 1851, adding new technical and medical training to the educational landscape.

periods.title: Constitutional Revolution
periods.summary: Protests led to a representative assembly, followed by royal resistance, armed struggle and restoration.

periods.title: War and dynastic replacement
periods.summary: Foreign occupation and the rise of Reza Khan weakened the monarchy; the Qajars lost the crown in 1925.

items.text: Qajar power emerged through a prolonged struggle after the Zand era. Agha Mohammad Khan defeated Lotf Ali Khan in 1794 and took the crown in 1796. His assassination in 1797 brought his nephew Fath Ali Shah to power. The dynasty’s beginning is therefore better understood as a sequence than as a single map date.

Wars with Russia transformed the northern frontier. The treaties of Golestan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828 confirmed major losses of Iranian-held territories in the Caucasus. Communities and trade routes were divided by a new international boundary. Several imported atlas outlines fail to keep pace with these changes.

The Constitutional Revolution brought merchants, clerics and reform-minded intellectuals into a struggle to limit arbitrary royal power. The first Majles assembled in 1906. Constitutional government faced a royal coup in 1908, was restored in 1909, and suffered another major reversal when the second Majles was dissolved in 1911. Agreement on a parliament did not mean agreement on every reform.

World War I brought foreign troops into Iran and further weakened the state. In 1921, Reza Khan’s Cossack forces entered Tehran and he became the dominant military figure. These events belong to the final Qajar years, even though this particular map record stops in 1920.

sections.title: Families, food and getting through the day

items.text: Extended families could share a compound, with married sons, their spouses and children living alongside older relatives. Wealth shaped the space: a rich household might have separate private and reception sections, while poorer families shared buildings and used curtains to divide a room. Family life did not look identical behind every doorway.

In the urban houses described by historian Shireen Mahdavi, toilets stood off the courtyard, with a water pitcher for cleansing. Wealthy compounds could have their own baths; other residents used public bathhouses. Water storage rooms could also keep perishable food cool. Plumbing arrangements depended strongly on the household’s resources.

Rooms changed jobs during the day. Bedding was folded away in the morning; at mealtimes, food was served on a cloth spread on the floor. Water and a basin were brought for washing fingers before and after eating. Bread could help scoop up food: part of the meal also did the work of a utensil.

A korsi made winter gatherings cozy: a low wooden frame stood over a heat source beneath a large quilt, with people sitting around it and warming their feet underneath. Tea, meals and games could occupy the top. It was a gathering place as well as a heater, and its history began long before the Qajars.

The new Russian frontier cut across Shahsevan winter pastures in the Moghan plain. Families and herds continued crossing it, provoking disputes with border authorities. Russia’s closure of the frontier to these nomadic groups in 1884 disrupted an established seasonal way of life. A line drawn between states could become a very practical problem for finding grazing.

Kerman’s expanding carpet industry linked local work to distant buyers. Its workshops employed people displaced from the countryside and many children under harsh conditions. Merchants often captured much of the profit, while imported textiles undermined other crafts, including shawl-making. Beautiful exported objects could conceal very unequal working lives.

Dar al-Fonun opened in Tehran in December 1851. Its subjects included military sciences, engineering, mining, medicine and pharmacy. The first recruitment notice sought teenage sons of elite families, but the actual intake was more mixed and students arrived with very different preparation. Some needed basic language and mathematics instruction before tackling advanced work.

The college provided a free daily lunch and two sets of clothes each year, one for summer and one for winter. Uniform colors distinguished students in different disciplines. Studies also included Persian, Arabic and French. School life combined new technical subjects with language learning, exams and a distinctly military sense of discipline.

Girls’ education followed several paths. Some attended traditional maktabs or learned at home; Assyrian, Armenian, Jewish, Zoroastrian and other communities developed schools, alongside new Muslim girls’ schools. A 1911 report counted 47 girls’ schools in Tehran with 2,187 pupils. These opportunities mattered, but they were far from universal access.

Smallpox vaccination developed unevenly. Crown Prince Abbas Mirza had his family vaccinated and encouraged medical learning; a Persian translation of John Cormick’s vaccination tract was printed in Tabriz in 1829. Print could carry practical health information as well as poetry and news. Acceptance and administration remained difficult, so publication alone did not guarantee protection.

By 1916, a vaccination center at Dar al-Fonun combined treatment with teaching. Medical students vaccinated people under professors’ supervision, learning techniques and possible complications while serving the city. Public-health administration was changing, although this one clinic cannot tell us how easily a family in a distant village obtained care.

sections.title: Pictures and a Persian writing sample

items.text: Qajar artists adopted lithography and photography while also changing older forms such as painted portraits. These technologies widened the ways pictures could be made and circulated. Royal images could look back to Iran’s earlier dynasties while presenting the ruler as a patron of new techniques and reform.

By the late nineteenth century, large religious paintings appeared in coffeehouses. Their subjects included the martyrdom of Husain at Karbala, also commemorated in Shiite passion plays. These portable canvases brought ambitious storytelling to public gathering places beyond the royal palace.

A painting now in the Metropolitan Museum shows Nasir al-Din Shah beside a cannon. Made in Iran around 1850 with watercolor, ink and gold on paper, it combines a carefully presented ruler with military equipment. The combination can be read as a display of royal authority, using paint and precious metal to give the ruler a commanding presence.

A silver coin from Isfahan, dated 1244 AH (1828-29), carries this Persian inscription: سكه فتحعلى شه خسرو صاحبقران. The Ashmolean translates it as “the coin of Fatḥ ‘Alī Shāh, Caesar of the fortunate conjunction.” The grand title linked the ruler to auspicious astrology. This wording survives on museum coin HCR18505.

ending.text: The map stops in 1920, but Qajar rule ended in 1925. On 31 October, the Majles deposed the dynasty; on 12 December, a constituent assembly transferred the crown to Reza Shah and his male heirs. The Pahlavi dynasty replaced the ruling house. Iran’s population, languages and communities continued through that political change.
